analysis.one_liner: Repeals taxes on medical device makers and health insurers while extending Medicare, Medicaid, and welfare programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: referred there on December 9, 2019, it got no hearing, no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently repeal the excise tax on medical devices and suspend the annual fee on health insurers, while also extending a batch of Medicare and Medicaid programs that help low-income seniors, safety-net hospitals, and community mental health clinics. It would also reauthorize the main federal welfare program (TANF) through 2024 under a new name, with stricter work requirements and new limits on how states can spend the money. It never received any committee action or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medical device manufacturers gain from a permanent repeal of their excise tax; health insurers gain from a multi-year suspension of the annual fee they owe under the Affordable Care Act. Ordinary people gain too: seniors and people with disabilities get continued Medicare outreach and counseling programs, married couples keep Medicaid protections that prevent a spouse from being impoverished when one enters a nursing home, safety-net hospitals avoid scheduled payment cuts, and community mental health clinics keep federal support. TANF families would get five more years of funded block grants and expanded child care money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device makers, insurers, and low-income patients

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2.3% excise tax on medical devices permanently, effective for sales after December 31, 2019.
Suspends the Affordable Care Act annual fee on health insurance providers, keeping it off for 2021 and 2022 before it resumes in 2023.
Makes permanent the reduction of the medical expense deduction floor from 10% to 7.5% of income, helping taxpayers with large out-of-pocket medical costs.

Extends Medicaid spousal impoverishment protections through December 2020, which keeps the at-home spouse from being stripped of income and assets when the other spouse needs long-term nursing home care paid by Medicaid.
Delays scheduled cuts to Medicaid payments to hospitals that serve many low-income patients (DSH reductions), pushing them from 2021-2025 back to a period starting December 2020.

Extends the Community Mental Health Services demonstration program through March 2021 and authorizes extra Medicare outreach funding for low-income beneficiary counseling programs, area agencies on aging, and disability resource centers.

Reauthorizes the TANF block grant (renamed the Jobs and Opportunity with Benefits and Services program) through fiscal year 2024, and increases the child care entitlement to about $2.9 billion for 2020 and $3.5 billion per year for 2021-2024.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the lost revenue from repealing the device tax and the insurer fee, which are real federal receipts. Some TANF families could lose aid under the bill's stricter rules: it requires 'universal engagement' in work activities, allows states to reduce benefits for families that don't comply, bans use of TANF funds for direct child care spending, caps eligibility-related spending at families below twice the poverty line, and prohibits benefits at any establishment that sells marijuana.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers via lost revenue; some TANF families

drawbacks.text: The two permanent tax repeals — the medical device excise tax and the health insurer fee suspension — forgo billions in federal revenue each year that otherwise comes from insurers and device manufacturers, shifting the cost to general taxpayers.

The welfare section tightens the program for poor families: it mandates that every work-eligible recipient engage in approved work activities, lets states cut benefits for those who don't comply, and prohibits states from spending TANF grants directly on child care services, which critics of similar proposals argued could force families out of assistance.
The bill prohibits using TANF funds to provide assistance to families with monthly income above twice the federal poverty line, narrowing who can be served.
Many Medicare and Medicaid 'extender' programs are continued only briefly (most through late 2020 or March 2021), creating repeated cliff-edge extensions rather than stable funding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a trade. It pairs genuine help for low-income patients, seniors, and safety-net providers with permanent tax relief for two industries, and a welfare reauthorization that adds money and case management while making benefits conditional on stricter work compliance. The device tax repeal and insurer fee moratorium are the items with the clearest concentrated-interest benefit; the patient-facing extenders are mostly short-term continuations of existing programs. Whether the TANF overhaul helps or hurts poor families depends heavily on how states implement the work requirements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Patrick Toomey introduced the bill in the Senate on December 9, 2019, joined by two Republican cosponsors including Sen. Mike Crapo.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken on the bill — it received no committee consideration, no floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, nothing in it took effect: device makers and insurers did not get the tax relief it offered, but neither did TANF work requirements tighten. The status quo prevailed for everyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill expired untouched in committee

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill combining health tax repeals, Medicare/Medicaid extenders, and a TANF reauthorization.

for.name: Second Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it two Republican cosponsors in total.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for Medicare, Medicaid, and tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 9, 2019 and never held a markup or advanced it; it died there without a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored the bill (one sponsor and two Republican cosponsors), but it never reached a floor vote, so no vote-based party split exists.

industries.note: The bill permanently repeals the excise tax on medical device sales, eliminating a tax the industry has long sought. The lost revenue comes out of the federal treasury, and the tax had been partly passed through to device prices.

The bill suspends the Affordable Care Act annual fee on health insurance providers for 2021 and 2022. Insurers save billions, though insurers typically passed much of that fee on to customers through premiums, so consumers saw some benefit too.

Delays scheduled Medicaid DSH payment cuts that disproportionately affect hospitals serving large numbers of uninsured and low-income patients; avoiding the cuts protects care access in poor communities.
Extends the Medicaid community mental health services demonstration through March 2021, keeping federal support for clinics serving people with serious mental illness.

The TANF section reauthorizes the block grant through 2024 but imposes universal work engagement, negotiated performance targets, penalties, and limits on using funds for direct child care, shrinking state flexibility in some areas while adding money for child care.
